attribution.note: Zitron's own words. He reports Anthropic's denial and says himself that it doesn't square with the complaints.

semantics.note: 'Inconsistent with' is a fair rendering of 'doesn't really square'. The claim is really an inference about why the regressions happened, which makes it causal, not a plain observation. The contract treats it the same way.

contract.note: The contract reads the line as scepticism about a specific denial and asks for evidence that the regressions were driven by demand. That is a fair, ordinary reading. Whether 'degrade models' covers product settings changes the result.

evidence.note: Dated Anthropic post with the denial. It sets the denial's scope but is a company statement and does not settle anything.
Original complaint from April 2. Shows users reported regressions starting in February, but does not show what caused them or that demand was a factor.

Anthropic's postmortem blames latency trade-offs, a caching bug and a prompt change. It is the company's own account, not an independent audit, so it can neither confirm nor rule out demand as a cause.

reviews.rationale: The complaints show regressions really happened. Anthropic's postmortem names causes other than demand, but it is a company disclosure. No independent deployment record ties the changes to demand, and none rules it out. The packet cannot show whether the denial was true or false.

attribution.note: Zitron presents this as his own view ('agrees with me'). The claim is about demand, not about what Bosa said.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps both mechanisms and makes no claim about size. Treating it as causal is right.

contract.note: Plain reading: both mechanisms added usage, with no magnitude required. That is a fair and ordinary reading of firm wording.

evidence.note: April 2026 report on Anthropic dropping subscription access for third-party tools, plus one user's account of heavier usage. Anecdotal and unmeasured.
June 2026 report on incentives to use more tokens. It describes a later period and contains no usage data.
July 2026 survey showing users are sensitive to price. It does not isolate the effect of subsidies or token-maxxing before the post.

reviews.rationale: The packet has anecdotes and later reporting that are consistent with both mechanisms. It has no usage comparison and no cost data showing that token-maxxing and subsidised access raised demand by the April 21 post. The evidence does not settle the causal claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion in his own post.

semantics.note: The normalised version drops 'effectively' and the clause about the two labs relying on infinite resources, but keeps the core majority claim. The 'infinite resources' part is rhetoric.

contract.note: Reading 'most' as more than half by count and 'front-ends' as companies mainly dependent on these models is ordinary and fair. The choice of population and period does drive the result.

evidence.note: Langfuse trace shares for October 2024 to September 2025. It measures usage, not a count of companies, and the period is before the target quarter. OpenAI's 55.3% share is not a majority-of-companies figure.

reviews.rationale: There is no representative company-level count for Q1 2026 showing whether most generative-AI firms mainly depend on OpenAI or Anthropic. The one item covers usage share in an earlier period. The 'infinite resources' clause is rhetoric and cannot be scored.

attribution.note: The claim that the figure doesn't add up is Zitron's own. Rao's affidavit is only what the claim is about.

semantics.note: The revised proposition keeps 'exceeding' and the March 9 date. It correctly frames the claim as an alleged inconsistency with reported annualized figures.

contract.note: Requiring incompatible constraints is an ordinary reading of 'does not make sense'. Zitron himself flagged 'exceeding', so reading it as a lower bound is not stretched against him.

evidence.note: The original declaration says cumulative revenue was 'exceeding $5 billion to date'. That is a lower bound, compatible with any larger total the run-rates might imply.
Secondary summary that repeats the filing's 'exceeded' wording. Its 'about a quarter' framing treats the lower bound as an exact figure, and it adds nothing independent.
Anthropic's $14B run-rate disclosure from February 2026. It is an annualized figure, a different metric from cumulative realized revenue, so it cannot simply be added up as revenue.

reviews.rationale: The affidavit gives only a lower bound on cumulative revenue. Any total that reported run-rates imply above $5B fits that bound, so there is no inconsistency. Zitron's objection only works if 'exceeding $5B' is treated as an exact total, or if annualized snapshots are added up as realized revenue. That matches the contract's contradiction condition.
